Les personnes racisées et la langue fran: Racialized People and the French Language: An Ambivalent Relationship
À l’occasion du Sommet de la francophoni: On the occasion of the Francophonie Summit, La Converse and Bondy Blog co-organized a conference titled “Parlons français” on October 3, 2024.
La conférence \"Parlons Français\" a réu: The “Parlons Français” conference brought together Emeline Odi, freelance journalist at Bondy Blog and member of the Association des Journalistes Antiracistes et Racisé·e·s; Anina Ciuciu, lawyer and founder of the collective L'École pour Tous; and Fatima Hammouch, Narratives manager at the feminist association Lallab. It was co-moderated by Sarah Ichou, director of Bondy Blog, and Lela Savić, founder and editor-in-chief of La Converse. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Au début du mois, <em>La Converse</em> s: Earlier this month, La Converse travelled to France to meet its European cousin: Bondy Blog. Three members of our team made the trip to build ties with this outlet, which shines a light on the Paris suburbs and on poorly or under-represented communities, and which was a source of inspiration when La Converse was created four years ago.
Nous avons rencontré une équipe passionn: We met a passionate and inspiring team, sat in on their editorial meeting, which is open to the public, shared our experiences… and organized a panel titled “Parlons français.” So what I’m offering you here is a look back at the rich exchanges of this first joint conference, with its committed panellists.
De la première rencontre avec le françai: From the first encounter with French, to the difficulties faced by minority communities, to the evolution of this language that brings us together, the discussion was deep and necessary.
Merci à tous ceux qui sont venus y assis: Thank you to everyone who came and fuelled the debate, thank you to the panellists and, of course, thank you to the Bondy Blog team for their welcome!
<strong>À l’occasion du 19e Sommet de la: On the occasion of the 19th Francophonie Summit, held in France on October 4 and 5, La Converse and Bondy Blog co-organized a conference titled “Parlons français” on October 3, 2024. The event brought forward testimonies and reflections on the French language and how racialized communities have made it their own.
L’expression “parler français” signifie: The expression “parler français” means speaking correctly, clearly and comprehensibly in the language. Conversely, we say someone “speaks French like a Spanish cow” when they struggle to make themselves understood. But in everyday speech, “parlons français” is also used to say that we want to have a frank, honest discussion, which is just what the three panellists at the conference did.
Pour ce premier événement conjoint autou: For this first joint event on the Francophonie, made possible by financial support from Quebec’s ministère de la Culture et des Communications, a panel of committed figures came together: Emeline Odi, freelance journalist at Bondy Blog and member of the Association des Journalistes Antiracistes et Racisé·e·s (AJAR); Anina Ciuciu, lawyer and founder of the collective L'École pour Tous; and Fatima Hammouch, Narratives manager at the feminist association Lallab.
Les modératrices, Sarah Ichou, directric: The moderators, Sarah Ichou, director of Bondy Blog, and Lela Savić, founder and editor-in-chief of La Converse, led this dialogue on the racial and linguistic issues surrounding French before an eclectic audience.
Le<em><l1>Bondy Blog</l1></em> est un mé: Bondy Blog is an online media outlet born during the urban uprisings of 2005, after the deaths of Zyed Benna and Bouna Traoré, two teenagers who were electrocuted inside an electrical substation where they had hidden to escape a police check. Nearly 20 years later, Bondy Blog continues to “tell the everyday stories of those who go unheard or whose voices are distorted, stigmatized, minoritized.” On both sides of the Atlantic, Bondy Blog and La Converse thus share the same mission: representing communities that are marginalized and made invisible in the media.

« C’est une langue de survie au départ p: “For me, it was a survival language at first”
Si la question de la <l1>francisation</l: While <l1>francization</l1> is often the issue that comes up most when immigrants or communities are discussed, the specific challenges racialized people face with the French language are in reality far broader. In France as in Quebec, the first of these is the encounter with a language that is foreign to them.
Fatima Hammouch, dont les parents ont ém: Fatima Hammouch, whose parents emigrated to France, experienced this painfully. “For me, it was a survival language at first. It was the administrative letters we received at home, where we didn’t speak French. My parents spoke only Amazigh, not even Arabic, so we were already a minority in Morocco. I learned the language through the administrative side, so I could read those papers and explain them to my parents, or make appointments at the CAF by pretending to be an adult on the phone when I was seven and a half… I had to master French because it was the link between my family and the outside world, the doctors and the teachers. I didn’t have time to appreciate it. I only really came to appreciate it much later, through books,” she says. Fatima Hammouch encountered French through a vocabulary that was, in the end, very “utilitarian.”
Cette première impression ne fait que se: That first impression was only reinforced when she sensed French society’s rejection of her mother. “At 12, I saw an abject debate about the headscarf on TV, when my mother wears one and I love it! I was angry to see her insulted and humiliated because of the image people have of her, and that she couldn’t defend herself because she didn’t master French well,” she recalls. That traumatic episode laid the foundation for the commitment of Fatima Hammouch, who describes herself as a “French and Moroccan Muslim woman.” Today, the woman who learned to love French literature is Narratives manager at Lallab, a feminist and antiracist association whose “goal is to make the voices of Muslim women heard and to defend their rights.”
Fatima Hammouch, responsable Narrations: Fatima Hammouch, Narratives manager for the association Lallab. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Anina Ciuciu aussi, a rencontré la langu: Anina Ciuciu also first met the French language in administrative forms, after leaving Romania, where she lived with her family in a Roma neighbourhood. “It’s my third language, because I’m Roma, then I learned Romanian before immigrating to Italy and finally to France,” says the writer and lawyer. Her parents had decided to leave the country after suffering racist discrimination and being fired.
Arrivée en France après un exil éprouvan: Arriving in France after a gruelling months-long exile across Europe, Anina Ciuciu discovered the stigma her community also faces there. “My commitment started a bit like Fatima’s. I describe it in my autobiography: I would see my mother hide when she came to pick me up from school, because she didn’t want the other kids to know I was Romani. It’s violent, it’s an injustice!” she says with a sigh.
Anina Ciuciu a ainsi transformé la honte: Anina Ciuciu thus turned shame and anger into fuel to denounce the prejudice Roma people still face today. “To change the reality of people like me, I decided to study law. When I passed the bar, I felt the need to go further, because racism is structural and change has to be too. That’s why we founded L'École pour Tous, which is an advocacy tool for obtaining concrete institutional change. For example, we got the law changed to fight racist refusals of school enrolment by going before the Conseil d'État, which ruled in our favour,” explains the woman who founded this association, which supports children and young people from marginalized groups (Roma, unaccompanied minors, residents of shantytowns or squats…).
Selon elle, la langue d’origine est un v: In her view, one’s original language is a vehicle for identity and resistance, particularly for minorities who are often made invisible by the dominance of French.

« On enrichit la langue par notre argot: “We enrich the language with our slang”
Si les pays de la francophonie partagent: While the countries of the Francophonie share a language, it clearly varies by country and era. In France and in Quebec, successive waves of immigration have contributed to the evolution of their adopted language.
Pigiste au <em>Bondy Blog</em>, Emeline: A freelancer at Bondy Blog, Emeline Odi specializes in sports journalism while campaigning for better representation of racialized people in the media through the Association des Journalistes Antiracistes et Racisé·e·s (AJAR): “With AJAR, we approach newsrooms to change how they represent racialized people, for example by emphasizing the physical features of a Black athlete when they don’t do that with others. In my own way, I try to change the narrative by working with outlets like Bondy Blog.”
Selon elle, l’évolution de la langue fra: In her view, the evolution of the French language is an important symbol, but not always a recognized one. “As young people from working-class neighbourhoods, we enrich the language with our slang, which ends up in the official dictionary, and yet society refuses the richness we can bring, or sees it as a corruption, when all living languages evolve. They refuse this contribution from Romani slang, from Ivorian mushi, or from Arabic, from all these languages that come from the former colonies,” says Emeline Odi.
Dans le public, ces paroles font réagir: In the audience, these words drew a reaction from Djibril, a young student: “It’s above all through French, francophone rap that the neighbourhoods have made the language their own and managed to win battles. 20 or 30 years ago, rap was seen as a zoulou (young thug, editor’s note) thing, and now rappers are winning awards at the Victoires de la musique. Maybe it’s not through literature or film, but we’ve managed to reclaim the language in our own way.”
Cela illustre la façon dont la culture p: This illustrates how popular culture can serve as a platform for voices that are often marginalized. Yet first-generation immigrants often favoured French over their mother tongue with their children, “probably so they’d integrate more easily,” according to Fatima Hammouch.
Emeline Odi regrette de ne pas pouvoir s: Emeline Odi regrets not being able to express herself in her parents’ original languages. “French is a language I came to love through literature. As a kid, I threw tantrums to get books, not toys, but I also feel the frustration of not speaking my parents’ languages. I noticed that my father made a point of speaking French at home, but never taught me the languages he speaks: Lingala and several other languages spoken in Congo, as well as Russian. It’s a bit frustrating for me,” says the journalist.
Un sentiment de perte d’une partie de le: The feeling of losing part of their identity resonates with the two other panellists. “French is the language I use the most, since I work in French and I wrote a book in French, but it’s extremely important to me to keep my mother tongue and to teach my daughter Romanes,” says Anina Ciuciu. “Historically, it’s a language of resistance for the Roma, because our oppressors didn’t understand it (the Roma suffered a genocide during the Second World War, editor’s note), so I think we need to preserve this endangered language. It’s very important for everyone who speaks a minority language in the face of French, the dominant language. It takes real effort to maintain our languages, because we forget that for most of the millions of people in the world who speak French, it isn’t their mother tongue,” says Anina Ciuciu.
Selon Fatima Hammouch, ce retour aux rac: According to Fatima Hammouch, this return to linguistic roots can only happen by restoring the prestige of minority cultures. “The Francophonie is often seen through a colonial aesthetic, where certain languages, like Arabic, are devalued. There is an eviction of the neighbourhoods and of minorities in order to maintain the francophone elite. The racialized Francophonie is voices like Leïla Slimani or Tahar Ben Jelloun, who, although talented, often come from an elite that maintains domination.” To counter negative stereotypes tied to a speaker’s origins, valuing linguistic diversity would therefore be a prerequisite.
Selim, contributeur au Bondy Blog. Photo: Selim, contributor to Bondy Blog. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Selim, un jeune contributeur du Bondy Bl: Selim, a young contributor to Bondy Blog, shares this analysis. “French is a living, evolving language, but when some people said Aya Nakamura shouldn’t sing at the Olympics because she doesn’t speak French, you can see that this enrichment is rejected. We should bring back narratives about languages and cultures, like Arabic, which for a long time was said to be an immigrant’s and poor person’s language, or all the other minority languages or those of former colonies,” says the young man, who plans a career in journalism.
Finalement, cette première conférence co: In the end, this first joint conference by Bondy Blog and La Converse allowed for a sharing of experiences as diverse as each person’s own history, yet as similar as the common patterns that bind all racialized people in their sometimes ambiguous relationship with French.
En conclusion, les trois intervenantes o: In conclusion, the three speakers emphasized the importance of “intersectional solidarity” and of fighting racism within racialized communities themselves, in order to build a Francophonie of inclusion that values all of its identities: “Instead of dividing us, we have to wage this fight together,” concludes Emeline.
